NSE   :   SUNPHARMA   |   BSE Code:   524715 Pharmaceuticals & Drugs 1 INTRODUCTION Sun Pharma started as a domestic branded-formulations player and scaled largely through acquisitions: US entry via Caraco (1998), Taro for US dermatology (FY10, fully absorbed FY24), DUSA for innovative medicines entry (FY13), and  Odomzo  and  Cequa  access via the Novartis and Ocular Technologies deals (FY17). Its 2014 Ranbaxy acquisition remains its largest deal to date, giving it generics scale and its OTC entry through Volini and Revital. Since the mid-2010s it has deliberately pivoted from commodity US generics toward patent-protected specialty medicines, a shift continuing through  Leqselvi ,  Unloxcyt , and now Organon. BUSINESS MODEL •  India Branded Formulations:  Prescription-led, highest-margin business with strong market leadership. •  US Formulations:  Generics and higher-margin Innovative Medicines, now the larger segment. •  Global Innovative Medicines:  Patent-protected portfolio driving high growth and margins. •  Emerging Markets & ROW:  Branded generics across 100+ countries, ensuring diversification. •  API Business:  Internal supply and external sales with backward integration. BRAND PORTFOLIO •  Specialty Portfolio:   Ilumya  (psoriasis),  Winlevi  (acne),  Cequa  (dry eye),  Odomzo  (oncology),  Leqselvi  (alopecia areata), and  Unloxcyt  (cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma). •  Consumer/OTC Portfolio:  Revital ( nutritionals ), Volini (topical analgesics),  Faringosept  (sore throat). •  Core Portfolio:  2,000+ molecules across psychiatry, cardiology, diabetology, dermatology, oncology, gastroenterology, and other therapeutic areas. PRODUCT ECOSYSTEM •  Dosage Forms:  Tablets, capsules, injectables, inhalers, ointments, creams, and liquids. •  Product Categories:  Generics, branded generics, specialty, OTC, ARVs, and APIs. •  Pipeline:   Fibromun  and  Nidlegy  nearing regulatory filing; GL0034 and MM-II in clinical trials. •  Post-Organon:  Expands portfolio with women's health, fertility, and biosimilars. Strategic Approach •  Specialty-led Mix Shift:  Focus on expanding higher-margin Innovative Medicines to offset US generic pricing pressure. •  Large-scale M&A:  Organon acquisition strengthens the specialty portfolio with minimal product overlap. •  Domestic Leadership:  37 new launches and market share growth to 8.4%, supported by global diversification. About The Company

EQUITY   RESEARCH   REPORT Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd. NSE   :   SUNPHARMA   |   BSE Code:   524715 Pharmaceuticals & Drugs 1 Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd. (NSE: SUNPHARMA) is India's largest pharma company and the largest Indian player in the US market. FY26 consolidated revenue grew 11.9% YoY to ~₹58,220 crore, EBITDA rose 16.1% to ~₹17,700 crore, and net profit grew 5% to ~₹11,479 crore. Stock trades at ~₹1,880–1,900 (market cap ~₹4.6 lakh crore, mid-July 2026), 52-week range ₹1,548–1,963, P/E ~38–39x, near debt-free, dividend payout ~34%. Thesis: a structural shift from commoditized US generics toward a higher-margin Global Innovative Medicines franchise (~21% of sales, scaling), anchored by a defensive India branded-formulations base (~33% of sales, #1 market share). The $11.75bn Organon acquisition, Sun Pharma's largest deal since Ranbaxy, is the key swing factor. It adds women's health, fertility, and biosimilars, and expands reach into Europe, China, and Latin America. •  Revenue:  ₹58,220 crore (+11.9% YoY); Net Profit: ₹11,479 crore (+5% YoY) •  India Formulations:  ₹19,290 crore (+14%), contributing 33% of sales •  US Formulations:  ~₹16,370 crore (-0.9%), contributing ~28.8% of sales •  Emerging Markets:  ~₹10,840 crore (+13.6%); Rest of World: ~₹8,330 crore (+14.4%) •  Innovative Medicines:  ~₹12,210 crore (20.7% of FY26 sales); US business crossed ₹8,600 crore •  Leqselvi  and  Unloxcyt  launched in the US during FY26 • India market share increased from  8.1%  to  8.4% ; 37 new products launched •  R&D Spend:  ₹3,554 crore (vs. ₹3,248 crore in FY25) •  Organon acquisition:  ~₹1.01 lakh crore deal; ~₹34,300 crore cash equity investment at US$14/share Executive Summary Key Highlights

NSE   :   SUNPHARMA   |   BSE Code:   524715 Pharmaceuticals & Drugs 1 Industry   Overview The global pharmaceutical industry, typically analysed across branded, generic, and specialty medicine segments, is projected to reach an estimated market size of approximately  US 1.76 trillion in 2026  based on direct industry estimates. More recent industry tracking values the baseline market at  US 2.225 to US 60.32 billion in 2026 . This specific figure is sourced from Mordor Intelligence, a reputable market research firm that provides a direct estimate for 2026. The global pharmaceutical industry's expanding size in 2026 reflects its critical role in worldwide disease management and healthcare.  Original branded medicines  dominate the market value, accounting for approximately  66% of the total global spending , primarily due to high-income developed markets. Additionally,  specialty medicines —used to treat chronic, complex, and rare diseases—make up a rapidly surging segment of the market and are expected to account for  43% of total global spending  by 2027 and 2028. Generic medicines and Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs)  make up a highly significant portion of the market's volume, driven by global cost-containment pressures and the need for affordable healthcare access. The  "Pharmerging" markets'  growth is particularly notable, as they are projected to expand at a rapid  10-13% CAGR  to reach US$ 400-430 billion by 2028, with China and India being the largest global volume contributors. This regional strength is underpinned by demographic shifts such as an aging population, rising per capita incomes, and robust government initiatives like India's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme to boost domestic manufacturing capabilities. Industry   Size  (2026 ) The global pharmaceutical industry is projected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 6%–9% from 2024 to 2028. This range is derived from recent global pharmaceutical market estimates, which reflect an upward revision in the outlook for medicine spending as the pandemic transitioned to an endemic phase and global medicine usage steadily expanded. The growth is underpinned by the increasing demand for chronic care, specialty treatments, and innovative therapies across various applications, with the market size expected to expand significantly. For instance, the global pharmaceutical market was valued at US 2.225 trillion and US$ 2.255 trillion by 2028. These figures indicate a robust market trajectory, driven by global demographic shifts such as an aging population, the rising prevalence of chronic lifestyle diseases, and sustained investments in high-value innovative treatments like oncology and immunology. By 2030, 1 in 6 people globally will be aged 60 or older, and the population of those aged 80 years or older is projected to triple to 426 million between 2020 and 2050, heavily driving the demand for age-related and chronic medications. Rise of Chronic & Lifestyle Diseases : Sedentary lifestyles, urbanization, and changing dietary habits are driving a rapid surge in Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs) like cardiovascular ailments and hypertension. Medicines to treat NCDs are projected to account for 85% of global spending, with diabetes care alone expected to reach nearly US$ 168 billion in revenues to become the third-largest therapy area globally by 2027. Specialty Medicines & Innovative Therapies : There is a massive shift toward advanced treatments for complex, chronic, and rare conditions, particularly in oncology, immunology, and endocrinology. Specialty medicines are expected to account for 43% of total global pharmaceutical spending by 2028, and will command over 55% of the total spending in developed markets . Government Support & Infrastructure Push : In India, robust government incentives are bolstering domestic manufacturing and reducing import dependence to solidify its position as the "pharmacy of the world". Key drivers include a Rs. 15,000 crore (US 7 billion) strategic push to elevate local Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) production capacity. Digital Health & AI Integration : The adoption of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and advanced analytics is revolutionizing the pharmaceutical value chain. These technologies are optimizing clinical trial designs, accelerating drug discovery, predicting supply chain models, and enabling personalized medicine, thereby driving immense productivity and new care outcomes. NSE   :   SUNPHARMA   |   BSE Code:   524715 Pharmaceuticals & Drugs 1 PORTER’S   FIVE   FORCES High Capital and Regulatory Requirement:  Entering the global pharmaceutical market requires massive financial investments in R&D (Sun Pharma consistently invests 6-8% of its annual revenues), complex manufacturing infrastructure, and strict, continuous adherence to global cGMP regulatory standards (like USFDA and EMA), which acts as a massive deterrent for new players. Economies of Scale and Vertical Integration:  Established leaders possess extensive vertically integrated operations—manufacturing both finished formulations and their own Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs)—which provides unmatched cost competitiveness and supply reliability that new entrants cannot easily replicate. Bargaining Power of Suppliers: Low to Medium Strategic Backward Integration:  Sun Pharma manufactures over 400 APIs in-house across 14 dedicated global facilities. This strategic backward integration significantly reduces its reliance on external suppliers for critical raw materials, ensuring supply reliability and insulating profit margins. Global Supply Chain Vulnerabilities:  While the company's massive scale allows for diversified sourcing, suppliers of non-substitutable and critical raw materials still hold some power, especially when global supply chains are disrupted by geopolitical tensions and economic downturns. Threat of New Entrants: Low Competitive Rivalry: High Hyper-Competitive US Generics Market:  The global generics space, particularly the US, is fiercely competitive. A faster pace of generic drug approvals by the USFDA, combined with multiple manufacturers targeting the same off-patent molecules, results in severe price erosion, forcing companies to continuously optimize costs and withdraw non-remunerative products. Fierce Battles in Emerging Markets:  In  pharmerging  markets (including India), competitive intensity between multinational pharmaceutical giants and deeply entrenched local players is incredibly high. Companies must continuously innovate, build strong brand equity with doctors, and rapidly launch complex or specialty products to defend and grow their market share.

This leads to an intensely competitive pricing environment characterized by severe off-invoice discounts and rebates Government-Mandated Price Controls:  Governments and institutional payers globally act as massive buyers. Faced with soaring healthcare deficits, they frequently enforce strict drug price controls, mandate periodic price cuts (as seen in Japan), and promote aggressive generic substitution to force down pharmaceutical prices. Generic and Biosimilar Competition:  For patented and specialty medicines, the loss of patent exclusivity immediately exposes them to highly affordable generic and biosimilar substitutes. Furthermore, the rapid pace of FDA approvals continuously introduces competing generic substitutes into the market. Shift Towards Preventative Care:  There is a growing global consumer shift towards self-care, wellness, and over-the-counter (OTC) alternative products, which can act as substitutes for traditional prescription therapeutics, though Sun Pharma actively mitigates this by aggressively expanding its own Global Consumer Healthcare business.

Appendix   –   Carbon   Credits Carbon   credits   are   measurable,   verifiable   emission   reductions   from   certified   climate   action   projects.   These   projects   reduce,   remove   or  avoid   greenhouse   gas   (GHG)   emissions.   But   they   also   bring   a   whole   host   of   other   positive   benefits,   for   example,   they   empower communities,   protect   ecosystems,   restore   forests   or   reduce   reliance   on   fossil   fuels.   Projects   must   adhere   to   a   rigorous   set   of   criteria   to  pass   verification   by   third- party   agencies   and   a   review   by   a   panel   of   experts   at   a   leading   voluntary   carbon   market   standard   like   Verra   or  Gold   Standard. How   prices   of   carbon   credits   change  ? There   are   a   number   of   reasons   prices   of   carbon   credits   vary,   for  instance: the   value   projects   deliver   beyond   carbon,   for   example   some   projects   empower  women   or   have   direct   impacts   on   people's   lives; varying   implementation   costs   depending   on   the   size   and   location   of   a   project; similarly   some   types   of   technology   are   more   expensive   than   others; carbon   pricing   regulations   can   affect  prices   in   the   voluntary   carbon   markets too; finally,   prices   are   driven   to   a   large   extent   by   supply   and   demand. While   the   voluntary   carbon   market   was   estimated   to   be   worth   about   $400   million  last   year,   forecasts   place   the   value   of   the   sector   between   $10- 25   billion   by   2030,  depending   on   how   aggressively   countries   around   the   world   pursue   their   climate  change   targets.

Appendix   –   Blue   Finance Indonesia's   dependence   on   Oceans With   more   than   17,500   islands,   108,000   kilometers   of   coastline,   and   three-quarters   of   its   territory   at   sea,   oceans   are   essential   to   Indonesia's  economic   prosperity   through   capture   fishing   and   aquaculture,   coastal   tourism,   marine   construction,   and   transportation.   Indonesia   has   the  second-largest   fishery   sector   in   the   world,   contributing   approximately   US$27   billion   to   the   country's   GDP   and   providing   7   million   jobs   and   more  than   half   of   the   country's   animal- based   protein   requirements.   The   marine   and   non- marine   tourism   industries   will   contribute   approximately  US$21   billion   to   the   nation's   GDP   in   2019   (WTTC   2020).   In   2016,   44   percent   of   foreign   tourists   participated   in   marine   and   littoral   (MAC)   tourism  activities   (Ministry   of   Tourism,   2016). Blue   Bonds   and   Blue   Loans   are   innovative   financing   instruments   that   allocate   funds   solely  for  ocean- friendly   initiatives   and   the   protection   of   vital   pure   water   resources.   In   general,   the  market   has   witnessed   the   exponential   development   of   sustainable   finance   and  the  emergence   of   a   variety   of   instruments   based   on   green   or   social   use- of- proceeds   or  sustainability   objectives. The   Sustainable   Blue   Economy   Finance   Principles   were   introduced   in   March   of   2018.   These  Principles   contemplate   the   conservation   and   use   of   oceans,   seas,   and   marine   resources   in  accordance   with   Environmental   and   Risk   Management   practices,   such   as   the   IFC   Performance Standards. Blue   Financing   Instruments

Distribution/Scale: Indonesia   is   an   archipelago   spreading   across   17,000   islands   with   greater   than   50%   of   residents   living   in   rural   areas.   Creating   products   that  can   grow   to   scale   is   challenging   from   a   distribution   standpoint.   At   MIMPI,   there   was   an   underlying   theme   that   in   order   for   products   to   be  not   only   successful   but   also   sustainable   in   Indonesia,   they   have   to   go   beyond   just   being   part   of   ‘corporate   social   responsibility.’ Developing   appropriate   products: Regularly   when   companies   enter   a   new   market,   they   try   to   leverage   off   of   products   or   ideas   that   worked   well   in   other   locations   in   which  they   operate.   As   I   mentioned   previously,   Indonesia   is   a   diverse   country   spread   across   17,000   islands   and   a   “one   size   fits   all”   strategy   could  prove   to   be   problematic.   It’s   especially   important   to   listen   to   the   consumers   and   ask   what   they   want   in   addition   to   providing   what  insurance   companies   think   they   need. Government  &   Regulation: Currently,   microinsurance   in   Indonesia   is   governed   by   the   same   laws   and   rules   as   traditional   insurance   because   there   are   no   current provisions   to   distinguish   ‘micro’   from   traditional.   The   trend   for   Indonesia,   similar   to   many   emerging   economies,   is   that   they   wait   for   the  demand   first   before   developing   and   establishing   regulations.   As   more   companies   have   begun   to   enter   the   microinsurance   stage, regulators   have   started   to   work   with   organizations   to   develop   an   effective   framework   for   regulation. Claims   Settlement: Developing   an   efficient   and   effective   way   to   settle   claims,   especially   in   a   rural   environment   with   an   already   low   profit   margin   product,   is  challenging.   Ongoing   due   diligence   or   claims   verification   audits   can   also   be   both   extremely   expensive   and   inefficient   in   this   environment.  The   claims   processing   and   settlement   is   the   end   service   provided   to   the   customer;   more   often   than   not,   the   client   needs   the   payment   to 	be   settled   quickly   in   order   to   reduce   the   impact   in   their   lives   of   whatever   the   event   may   be. Source :   IBEF; McKinsey 02 RESEARCH ABSTRACT This report examines the historical evolution of the healthcare and pharmaceutical sectors, current market dynamics, and future growth pathways shaped by digital transformation, changing consumer behaviour, sustainability priorities, and evolving supply chains. The global healthcare industry is shifting from traditional, craft-based models to hyper-connected, AI-enabled ecosystems, with 90% of executives citing digital transformation as their top priority. Despite a steep patent cliff, segments like consumer healthcare ($245 billion, 7-8% CAGR) and next-generation therapies (9% CAGR) show strong growth, driven by generative AI, virtual health, and mega blockbuster drugs like GLP-1 therapies that is $25 billion opportunity in the US alone. Key trends include "China + 1" supply chain realignment, direct-to-patient commercial models, and agentic AI adoption. India's healthcare sector, is projected to $320 billion by 2028. This is backed by a strong pharmaceutical base $57.61 billion in 2025, growing to $79.74 billion by 2031 (5.74% CAGR), with domestic sales of $27.97 billion in FY26, up 8.8% YoY and a growing medical devices market, from $16.97 billion in 2025 to a projected $26.66 billion by 2031 (7.82% CAGR), alongside rising pharma exports of $31.11 billion in FY26. Despite structural challenges like high out-of-pocket expenditure and infrastructure gaps, India is repositioning from "pharmacy of the world" to an innovation-led "pharma powerhouse" under the Viksit Bharat 2047 vision.
